newsitem.title: USA: "Anaconda" slithers to top of U.S. box office.
newsitem.headline: "Anaconda" slithers to top of U.S. box office.

text.p: "Anaconda" overcame lukewarm reviews to slide into the top spot at the U.S. box office in its opening weekend, according to studio estimates released on Sunday.
The throwback to horror b-movies, starring Jon Voight, Jennifer Lopez and rapper Ice Cube, earned about $16.5 million during the Friday to Sunday period.
According to a spokesman for Columbia Pictures, the Sony Corp. -owned studio that released the picture, it marks the biggest non-holiday opening in April.

The top 10 contained one other new entry, "Grosse Pointe Blank" at fourth, and one re-entry as "Scream" entered its discount run. Last weekend's No. 1, "Liar Liar," slipped to second in its fourth weekend with $14.3 million. "The Saint," which opened in second last weekend, was third this time with $11.2 million.

"Anaconda," about a 40-foot snake on the loose in the Amazon, seemed to polarize critics. A Variety poll of reviewers in New York, Los Angeles, Chicago and Washington DC showed that eight liked it, 13 did not and eight were mixed. While influential critics Gene Siskel and Roger Ebert were favorable, the Los Angeles Times said it was unintentionally amusing.
The movie's average of $6,718 from 2,456 screens was the highest in the top 10.

Jim Carrey's "Liar Liar" has now earned about $119.8 million after 24 days in release. This weekend, it slipped just 22 percent from the weekend before, and averaged $4,965 from 2,880 screens. The movie is released by Universal Pictures, a unit of Seagram Co. Ltd..

"The Saint," starring Val Kilmer as master thief Simon Templar, has a 10-day total of $31.6 million. It slipped 31 percent this weekend and averaged $4,573 from 2,449 screens, an increase of 142 screens from the week before. The movie is released by Paramount Pictures, a unit of Viacom Inc.

"Grosse Pointe Blank," a well-reviewed romantic comedy starring John Cusack as a hitman who attends his high school reunion, opened in fourth with $7.0 million. It averaged a promising $5,705 from 1,227 screens.

The movie played well with "review-sensitive, college and sophisticated audiences," said Phil Barlow, president of Walt Disney Co.'s Buena Vista Pictures distribution arm. The Variety poll showed that 27 critics liked it, five did not and seven were mixed.
"Because it's a good movie and because we didn't get greedy and rush it out, I think it's going to be there for a while," Barlow said.

Columbia's "The Devil's Own," a thriller starring Brad Pitt and Harrison Ford, fell 39 percent and two places to fifth in its third weekend with $4.3 million. Its 19-day tally is $35.7 million. It averaged $1,826 from 2,355 screens.

Returning to the top 10 in ninth position was "Scream," the holiday box office hit from Disney's Miramax Films. Now playing in discount theaters, the movie rang up $2.0 million at the weekend, which takes its total to $88.6 million.
